personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Harry is defined by several interlocking traits: a dry, sardonic wit deployed quietly (calling Dudley's gang 'a bit stupid,' thinking Dudley looks like 'a pig in a wig,' silently comparing the boa constrictor's boredom to his own life); a baseline of patient, resigned endurance under Dursley mistreatment rather than overt anger; genuine, unaffected curiosity about the magical world (the rapid-fire questions to Hagrid, the wide-eyed wonder in Diagon Alley, the strategic thinking during the trio's underground adventure); instinctive physical bravery that surprises even himself (jumping on the troll's neck, flying after Malfoy without hesitation, grabbing Quirrell's face); deep insecurity about whether he truly belongs or deserves his fame (the extended worry before the Sorting, the stammered admission to Hagrid 'I don't think I can be a wizard,' the repeated fear of being 'the worst in the class'); and an emotionally restrained but powerfully felt longing for family (the Mirror of Erised scenes, the photographs). His voice in the books is notably understated: he rarely shouts, uses interior monologue heavily, and expresses strong emotions through small gestures rather than speeches. He also has a specifically bookish form of clever observation — noticing logical inconsistencies, asking precise follow-up questions — that makes him an active thinker rather than a passive reactor.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core personality profile recognizably well. Daniel Radcliffe's Harry is similarly quiet, observant, and reactive rather than bombastic. Key moments of understated wit survive: the wry 'I'm not going home — not really' at the film's close; the dry 'Anytime' to the escaping boa constrictor; the calm, collected 'I think I can tell the wrong sort for myself, thanks' to Malfoy. The insecurity before the Sorting ('Not Slytherin, not Slytherin — please, not Slytherin, anything but Slytherin') is directly preserved and even slightly amplified in delivery. The instinctive bravery on the broomstick and in the underground chambers is intact. His wonder and curiosity in Diagon Alley are conveyed visually. The quiet longing before the Mirror of Erised — 'Mum? Dad?' — is genuinely moving and faithful. However, several specific traits are compressed or lost. The book's extensive interior monologue — Harry's habitual self-questioning, his pattern of reasoning through events quietly before acting — is largely absent, replaced by visual storytelling. His sardonic inner voice (the pig-in-a-wig observation, the extended empathetic reasoning with the boa constrictor about shared experiences of confinement) does not fully translate. In the film, the snake scene is more abbreviated and slightly more whimsical in tone; in the book, Harry draws an explicit and melancholy parallel between the snake's captivity and his own. His self-deprecating insecurity is present but softer — the book Harry spends considerable time convinced he will be the worst student in the class and that Hagrid has made a mistake; the film Harry's self-doubt is briefer and less textured. His quiet, private emotional register — especially around his parents — is mostly preserved in the Mirror scenes but is less layered than the book, where it builds across multiple nights of obsessive return.
personality_voice.difference: The main losses are: (1) the richness of Harry's interior monologue and self-analysis, which in the books constitutes a major dimension of his voice; (2) his specifically dry, observational humour as a private coping mechanism; (3) the full depth of his insecurity, which in the books is persistent and self-undermining over multiple chapters; (4) his empathetic identification with marginalised figures (the boa constrictor parallel is thematically truncated in the film). These are not catastrophic alterations — the dominant traits survive — but they represent a genuine simplification of texture.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality is intact. The adaptation compression is real but does not transform Harry into a different character. The penalty is moderate: the film version is recognisably the same Harry, but the secondary layer of insecurity, dry wit, and interior complexity is thinned. Score placed in the 18–22 range, toward the higher end because the most important traits (bravery, curiosity, quiet endurance, emotional longing for family, resistance to Slytherin, fairness to friends) are all preserved with specific evidence.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Harry is the structural centre of every scene he inhabits. He is the primary driver of the investigative plot: he notices the Gringotts vault number in the Prophet, he initiates the conversation with Hagrid about the package, he interprets Snape's injury independently, he stakes out Snape and Quirrell in the forest, he argues for going through the trapdoor, he reasons through the Mirror of Erised to extract the Stone, he physically holds Quirrell's face to destroy him. He also drives key relational beats: he reaches out first to Ron on the train (sharing all his sweets, initiating the friendship), he independently decides to rescue Hermione from the troll before Ron has fully committed, and he is the one who finally confronts Quirrell alone. His agency in the climax is total — he is the only one who goes forward beyond the chess room.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film largely preserves Harry's narrative centrality. He drives the Quidditch subplot, the forest investigation, the Gringotts recognition, and the climactic descent. The chess room agency is intact in structure: Harry orders the final strategy, moves to checkmate, and gives Ron the decision to sacrifice himself. The Mirror room confrontation is preserved with Harry lying to Quirrell, feeling the Stone appear, and using touch to destroy Quirrell. The troll rescue — Harry jumping on the troll's neck — is preserved and gives him active agency alongside Ron. However, two meaningful transfers occur. First, in the books it is Harry who notices and interprets Snape's wound after the Quidditch match, then explicitly theorises that Snape let the troll in as a diversion; in the film this reasoning is partly preserved but delivered in dialogue where Hermione contributes more equally to the deduction. The scene where Harry goes to Snape's office and overhears the injury (a solo act of agency in the book) does not appear in the theatrical film. Second, the book's extended multi-night Mirror obsession — during which Harry independently reasons about the Stone retrieval method, builds on Dumbledore's warning, and makes active decisions — is compressed. The film cuts the extended obsession (listed as cut material), so Harry's development of self-knowledge around the mirror is less active. These are meaningful reductions but not wholesale transfers.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The most significant agency reduction is the absence of Harry's solo investigation of Snape's wound (book-only), which in the book gives Harry key independent deductive reasoning that he then shares with the trio. In the film, the Snape-is-suspicious thread is more collaboratively arrived at. The mirror obsession being cut also removes several nights of Harry making active choices (to return, to reflect, to reason). Neither is a full transfer to another character, but both reduce his independent investigative agency.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Role is essentially identical — Harry is the protagonist and structural driver throughout. Agency is reduced in the investigative thread (Snape's wound scene cut, mirror obsession cut) but not to a degree that reassigns his function. The role penalty is minor; the agency penalty is moderate. Score in the 14–17 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Harry's motivations in Book 1 are layered: (1) a fundamental desire to belong and be normal, paradoxically combined with (2) a longing to be extraordinary and special in a world that will accept him; (3) a fierce protectiveness of friends (troll scene, warning Neville, standing up to Malfoy on Ron's behalf); (4) a deep, grief-inflected need to understand and connect with his dead parents, which drives the Mirror behaviour and his emotional engagement with his history; (5) a moral instinct that specific wrongs must be addressed regardless of personal cost (going after the Stone despite being likely to be expelled). His internal conflict is most vivid around the Mirror: he knows he should stop returning, Ron and Dumbledore warn him, but his grief-driven hunger for family is powerful enough to override reason. There is also a conflict between wanting to be unremarkable (his constant embarrassment at fame) and wanting to prove himself (the Quidditch tryout, standing up to Malfoy, going after Quirrell alone). His decision to confront Quirrell is explicitly motivated by a sense of moral obligation — if Voldemort returns, everyone suffers — rather than heroism or self-interest.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the dominant motivations clearly. The belonging/family need is expressed through the Mirror scene ('Mum? Dad?') and the closing line ('I'm not going home — not really'). The protectiveness of friends is shown in the troll scene and the chess room. The moral obligation to stop Quirrell/Voldemort is stated explicitly before the descent ('if Voldemort gets the Stone, he comes back and everyone suffers'). The discomfort with fame is present in his reaction to the Leaky Cauldron welcome and his quiet manner throughout. However, the internal conflict around the Mirror — the full psychological weight of Harry choosing to keep returning despite knowing it is harmful, the way it temporarily makes him forget about the Stone and Voldemort (explicitly stated in the book) — is only partially present due to the cut of the extended mirror obsession scenes. In the theatrical film, Harry visits the mirror twice and is redirected by Dumbledore; the psychological pull is communicated but not dramatised over time. The conflict between wanting normalcy and wanting to prove himself is present but lightly drawn; the film Harry is more straightforwardly brave without the undercurrent of self-doubt about whether he deserves his place.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The Mirror obsession scenes being cut removes the clearest expression of Harry's internal conflict (grief vs. reason, wanting family vs. needing to act). The self-doubt motivation ('I bet I'm the worst in the class,' 'Hagrid must have made a mistake') is present but compressed. The core motivations are correctly identified, but the internal conflict dimension is underexpressed.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but not wrong. The film version is consistent with the book version; it simply removes some of the evidence for internal conflict. Score in the 11–13 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Harry's arc in Book 1 is precisely defined: he moves from a child with no identity, no belonging, no history, and no power to a young wizard who has claimed an identity, chosen a community, proven his courage, and accepted his past. The key turning points are: (1) learning he is a wizard and has a place in the world; (2) choosing Gryffindor over Slytherin (which the Sorting Hat offers) — a values-defining act; (3) the Mirror of Erised confrontation, which teaches him the danger of dwelling on dreams and that he must live in the present; (4) the encounter with Quirrell/Voldemort, in which he discovers his mother's sacrifice is literally protective, that love is his most powerful inheritance, and that he is capable of active courage against the worst evil; (5) the epilogue beat where he returns to the Dursleys but now from a position of self-knowledge and belonging ('I'm not going home — not really'). The arc is not about Harry becoming more powerful; it is about Harry becoming more himself.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film traces this arc faithfully in its broad structure. The identity discovery (wizard reveal, the Leaky Cauldron welcome, Diagon Alley), the Sorting Hat choice (preserved in full, with Harry's whispered 'not Slytherin'), the Mirror lesson (Dumbledore's explanation is preserved nearly verbatim), the climactic self-sacrifice beat (Harry choosing to go on alone), and Dumbledore's love-as-protection explanation are all present. The closing line ('I'm not going home — not really') seals the arc cleanly. The arc is compressed — the Mirror obsession turning point is truncated — but the key beats are hit. The one meaningful arc step that is partially reduced is the Mirror sequence: in the books, the obsession and Dumbledore's intervention together constitute a crucial lesson about the difference between dreaming about the past and choosing to live in the present, and Harry applies this lesson directly when he uses the mirror to get the Stone (he wants to find it but not use it). The film preserves this logically but the emotional journey to get there is shorter.
character_arc.difference: The arc's turning points are present and in the right order. The Mirror of Erised turning point is compressed (cut extended obsession). The final arc resolution is intact. No false arc is invented.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Arc is compressed but faithful. The compression does not alter Harry's trajectory or endpoint. Score in the 11–13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Harry's four key relationships in Book 1 are: (1) Ron — a rapid, natural friendship built on mutual recognition, Ron's knowledge of the wizarding world supplementing Harry's wonder, their shared outsider status (Ron's poverty, Harry's deprivation), and genuine warmth. Harry initiates generosity (buying all the sweets, sharing pasties, trying to comfort Ron about Scabbers). (2) Hermione — a more complex dynamic: initial mild irritation at her know-it-all manner, evolving into genuine respect and affection after the troll incident. Harry specifically defends her ('she needs to sort out her priorities' — notably Ron, not Harry). (3) Hagrid — a surrogate parent/mentor relationship carrying significant emotional weight: Hagrid is the first person to ever show Harry unconditional warmth, gives him his birthday cake, buys him Hedwig, reassures him before Hogwarts. (4) The Dursleys — an oppressor/victim dynamic that establishes Harry's baseline deprivation and his learned resilience. A fifth significant relationship is Harry's connection to his dead parents, mediated through the mirror, through Hagrid's stories, and through Ollivander's revelation about the twin wands.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Ron friendship is well established: the train compartment scene, the Quidditch support, the chess room sacrifice. The dynamic is warm and natural, though the book's detailed texture of mutual recognition (Harry noting he finds Ron as interesting as Ron finds him, the extended conversation about wizard families) is compressed. The Hermione relationship develops correctly through irritation to alliance after the troll; the film preserves the arc but the specific warmth Harry shows toward her — his quiet defensiveness of her — is less textured because the cut 'birth of the Golden Trio' scene (where Harry explicitly tells Ron Hermione was upset and that Hermione covered for them) removes a beat of Harry's emotional attentiveness. The Hagrid relationship is well served by the film — the birthday cake, Hedwig, the hug at the station are all present. The Dursley dynamic is established but the book's granular portrait of daily degradation (the cupboard under the stairs as bedroom, the systematic exclusion, the specific history of neglect) is abbreviated; this matters because it is the foundation that makes Harry's longing for belonging emotionally urgent. The parents relationship via the mirror is present and affecting.
key_relationships.difference: No major relationship dynamic is reversed or falsified. The main losses are textural: (1) the specific intimacy of the Harry-Ron train conversation (the book spends much more time on their mutual curiosity and warmth); (2) Harry's quiet emotional attentiveness toward Hermione after the troll (partially cut); (3) the full weight of the Dursley oppression as the context for all of Harry's emotional hunger. These are compressions rather than distortions.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationships are mostly faithful. Some compression, no major distortion. Score in the 7–8 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Harry's complexity in Book 1 rests on several specific textures: (1) his capacity for dark humour as a coping mechanism for his deprivation; (2) the genuine moral ambiguity of being famous for something he cannot remember and did not choose, and his discomfort with the gap between reputation and self-knowledge; (3) his empathetic identification with the marginalised — the boa constrictor, Neville, Hagrid (he defends Hagrid to Malfoy with cold fury: 'I think he's brilliant'), Ron's poverty — which is consistent and characterising; (4) the Mirror obsession as a portrait of grief and self-deception, showing Harry capable of rationalisation and compulsive behaviour; (5) his specifically unglamorous life pre-Hogwarts, rendered in fine-grained detail (the spiders in the cupboard, the taped glasses, the hand-me-down clothes, the systematic exclusion from birthday trips), which make his subsequent wonder and loyalty comprehensible; (6) the small flashes of rule-breaking pragmatism (trying to curse Dudley with the books in Diagon Alley, flying after Malfoy despite the rule, going through the trapdoor) that distinguish him from a simple hero.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: Several of these nuances survive intact: the rule-breaking pragmatism is well shown; the defence of Hagrid against Malfoy ('I think he's brilliant') is preserved verbatim and with the right cold tone; the empathetic connection to Neville (the Chocolate Frog gift, 'you're worth twelve of Malfoy') is preserved. The discomfort with fame is present. However, important nuances are reduced or absent. The boa constrictor scene loses the explicit parallel Harry draws between the snake's confinement and his own: in the book, Harry's empathy is based on a directly articulated identification ('it was worse than having a cupboard as a bedroom'); in the film, the conversation is warmer but the self-revelatory parallel is absent. The pre-Hogwarts deprivation detail — the cupboard, the spiders, the systematic material neglect — is shown but abbreviated; the film establishes Harry's poor conditions but does not dwell on the systematic psychological dimensions (being spoken about as if not present, being forbidden to ask questions) that make his subsequent reactions emotionally legible. The Mirror obsession being cut removes the clearest window into Harry's vulnerability to self-deception and grief. The Potions class scene — in which Harry maintains dignity under Snape's targeted humiliation — is present in the film but the book's extended version shows Harry's specific cognitive resilience (he has looked through his books, he is clearly not unprepared, Snape's attack is pure theatre) more clearly. The cut 'Dudley's uniform' scene removes a small but characterising beat of Harry's weary, resigned humour.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The cumulative effect of these cuts is that the film Harry is slightly simpler: more straightforwardly brave and reactive, less burdened by grief, less specifically formed by deprivation, and with less visible interior complexity. The character is not reduced to a single trait, but the 'second layer' — the texture that distinguishes a fully realised character from a well-executed sketch — is noticeably thinner. The cuts primarily affect: the empathy-born-from-personal-suffering dimension, the grief-as-vulnerability dimension, and the dry-wit-as-coping dimension.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character retains substantial complexity: multiple motivations, clear flaws, genuine relational warmth, and some internal contradiction. The losses are real but do not flatten Harry to a single function. Score in the 10–11 range.

Harry's explicit self-identification with the boa constrictor's captivity ('worse than having a cupboard as a bedroom') — present in books, truncated in film
Harry's persistent, multi-chapter insecurity about being 'the worst in the class' — present in books, compressed in film
Harry's solo investigation of Snape's staffroom wound (going alone to retrieve his book, overhearing Snape's injury) — present in books, absent in theatrical film
Harry's multi-night Mirror of Erised obsession, including his rationalisation, Ron's worry, and his temporary abandonment of the Stone investigation — cut from theatrical release
Harry's attempt to acquire a curses-and-countercurses book in Diagon Alley to curse Dudley — present in books, absent in film
Harry's specific daily deprivation detail (systematic psychological exclusion by Dursleys, forbidden to ask questions) — present in books, abbreviated in film
The 'birth of the Golden Trio' bathroom scene — cut from theatrical release; removes Harry's specific emotional attentiveness to Hermione

score_caps_applied: Cap 1 (above 85 requires no major complexity loss) considered and applied: mirror obsession scenes cut, boa constrictor self-identification reduced, interior monologue largely absent — these represent meaningful complexity losses, keeping score below 85

Cap 7 (above 75 requires no transferred core agency) examined: no full transfers identified, so this cap is not binding; however, the solo Snape-wound investigation being cut does reduce independent agency meaningfully and contributes to placing the score in the high 70s rather than above 80
key_observations: The film portrays Harry Potter faithfully in all structurally essential respects: his dominant personality traits, his arc from obscurity to identity, his key relationships, his central motivations, and his climactic agency are all preserved with specific, direct evidence. The adaptation earns a solid score. The penalty is driven primarily by cumulative compression: the film's Harry lacks the richly textured interior monologue that is a defining feature of the books, the Mirror of Erised obsession scenes (which constitute the most psychologically complex portrait of Harry in the first book) are cut from the theatrical release, and the specifically empathy-born-from-shared-suffering dimension of his personality — most visible in his identification with the boa constrictor and his persistent insecurity — is lighter. These losses do not transform him into a different character, but they do produce a Harry who is somewhat simpler, more reactive, and less explicitly burdened by the specific weight of his pre-Hogwarts deprivation. The final score of 79 reflects a portrayal that is substantially faithful, notably well-cast and well-performed, but measurably thinner than the source character in complexity and interiority.
